Week 1: Construction Payroll Fundamentals

Learning Objectives

By the end of this week, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish between union and non-union payroll systems and their unique requirements
  • Navigate multi-state payroll complexities including withholding and reciprocity agreements
  • Understand and implement prevailing wage requirements for government contracts
  • Ensure compliance with the Davis-Bacon Act and related labor standards
  • Prepare accurate certified payroll reports meeting federal and state requirements
  • Account for fringe benefits in both financial statements and payroll compliance
  • Design payroll systems that support project-based cost tracking and reporting

Introduction: The Unique Challenge of Construction Payroll

Construction payroll represents one of the most complex areas of construction accounting. Unlike typical business payroll, construction companies must track:

  • Multiple job sites across different states and jurisdictions
  • Various pay rates for different projects (prevailing wage vs. standard rates)
  • Union vs. non-union classifications with different benefit structures
  • Craft-specific requirements for different trades and skill levels
  • Detailed reporting for government contracts and compliance audits
  • Complex benefit allocations including health insurance, retirement, and training funds

Industry Statistics

Key Construction Payroll Facts:

  • Payroll typically represents 25-40% of total construction costs
  • 50% of construction companies face payroll compliance issues annually
  • Average penalty for Davis-Bacon violations: $8,500 per violation
  • Multi-state operations increase payroll complexity by 300%
  • Union contractors spend 40% more time on payroll administration

Section 1: Union vs. Non-Union Payroll Systems

Understanding Union Construction

Union construction involves collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) that dictate wages, benefits, work rules, and payment structures. Approximately 13% of construction workers in the United States are union members, but union contractors perform about 35% of commercial construction by dollar value.

Collective Bargaining Agreements (CBAs)

A CBA is a legally binding contract between the employer and the union that specifies:

  • Base wage rates by classification and experience level
  • Fringe benefit contributions to various funds and programs
  • Work rules including overtime, shift differentials, and working conditions
  • Reporting requirements for hours worked and wages paid
  • Grievance procedures for handling disputes
  • Jurisdictional rules determining which union performs which work

Example: Union Carpenter CBA Structure

Local 123 Carpenters Union - 2024 Agreement

Base Wage Rate: $42.50 per hour

Fringe Benefits (per hour worked):

Health & Welfare Fund$8.75
Pension Fund$6.50
Apprenticeship Training Fund$0.85
Industry Advancement Fund$0.45
Vacation/Holiday Fund$2.75
Supplemental Dues (2%)$0.85
Total Package Rate$62.65/hour

Overtime Provisions:

  • 1.5x base rate for hours over 8 per day or 40 per week
  • 2.0x base rate for Sundays and holidays
  • Fringe benefits paid at straight time regardless of overtime

Union Payroll Processing Workflow

Union payroll follows a specific process to ensure compliance with CBAs:

  1. Timekeeping: Track hours by project, classification, and union
  2. Rate Determination: Apply correct base wage and fringe rates per CBA
  3. Calculate Gross Pay: Regular hours + overtime at appropriate multipliers
  4. Calculate Fringes: Multiply total hours by fringe benefit rates
  5. Process Deductions: Federal/state taxes, union dues, working dues
  6. Generate Checks: Net pay to employee, fringe remittances to funds
  7. Fringe Remittance: Submit payments to various benefit funds with reports
  8. Union Reports: Provide required reporting to union locals

Union Payroll Journal Entries

Let's examine how to record union payroll transactions properly:

Example: Recording Union Payroll

Scenario: ABC Construction pays 10 union carpenters for Week 1 of January 2025. Each carpenter worked 40 regular hours at the rates shown in the previous CBA example.

Calculations:

  • Total hours: 10 employees × 40 hours = 400 hours
  • Base wages: 400 hours × $42.50 = $17,000
  • Fringe benefits: 400 hours × $20.15 = $8,060
  • Total payroll cost: $25,060

Non-Union Payroll Systems

Non-union construction payroll is typically simpler but still requires careful tracking and compliance:

Key Characteristics:

  • More flexible pay structures determined by employer
  • Simpler benefit administration (often centralized)
  • No union reporting requirements
  • Still must comply with prevailing wage on government projects
  • May use piece rate or production-based pay
  • Greater flexibility in overtime and shift arrangements

Example: Non-Union Carpenter Pay Structure

XYZ Construction - Non-Union Rates 2024

Carpenter Classifications:

LevelBase RateBenefits (% of wages)
Apprentice (0-2 years)$18.50/hr15% ($2.78/hr)
Journeyman (2-5 years)$26.00/hr20% ($5.20/hr)
Master Carpenter (5+ years)$34.50/hr25% ($8.63/hr)
Foreman/Lead$38.00/hr28% ($10.64/hr)

Benefits Package (Employer Costs):

  • Health insurance: Company contributes $650/month per employee
  • 401(k) match: 3% of wages (voluntary employee contribution)
  • Paid time off: Accrual based on hours worked
  • Workers' compensation: Included in percentage
  • Payroll taxes: Included in percentage

Total Package Comparison:

  • Union Master Carpenter: $62.65/hour fully loaded
  • Non-Union Master Carpenter: $43.13/hour fully loaded ($34.50 + $8.63)
  • Difference: Union premium of $19.52/hour (45% higher)

Common Pitfall: Mixing Union and Non-Union Workers

Many contractors make the critical mistake of using both union and non-union workers on the same project without proper procedures:

  • Legal Issues: May violate collective bargaining agreements
  • Project Issues: Can create jurisdictional disputes and work stoppages
  • Labor Relations: Damages relationships with unions for future projects
  • Best Practice: Keep projects clearly designated as union or open shop

Section 2: Multi-State Payroll Complexities

Construction companies frequently work across state lines, creating significant payroll tax compliance challenges. Each state has different rules for:

  • Income tax withholding
  • Unemployment insurance
  • Workers' compensation requirements
  • Temporary worker provisions
  • Reciprocity agreements

State Income Tax Withholding Rules

The fundamental question for multi-state operations: Which state's income tax should be withheld?

General Rules:

  1. Work Location Rule: Withhold tax for the state where work is performed
  2. Residence Rule: May also need to withhold for employee's home state
  3. Reciprocity Agreements: Some states have agreements to simplify withholding
  4. Convenience Rule: A few states tax income even when employee works remotely

Example: Multi-State Withholding Scenarios

Scenario 1: Simple Case with Reciprocity

Employee lives in Virginia, works on project in Maryland

  • Maryland and Virginia have reciprocity agreement
  • Employee completes Form MW507 (Maryland exemption)
  • Withhold Virginia state tax only
  • Report wages to both states

Scenario 2: No Reciprocity Agreement

Employee lives in Texas (no state income tax), works in Colorado

  • No reciprocity between Texas and Colorado
  • Withhold Colorado state tax on wages earned in Colorado
  • Employee may claim credit on Colorado return if Texas later imposes tax

Scenario 3: Multiple Work States

Employee lives in Pennsylvania, works on projects in PA, NJ, and DE

  • Track days/wages by state
  • Withhold each state's tax on wages earned in that state
  • Pennsylvania: 40 days = $12,000 wages
  • New Jersey: 35 days = $10,500 wages (no reciprocity with PA)
  • Delaware: 25 days = $7,500 wages
  • File quarterly returns in all three states

State Reciprocity Agreements

Reciprocity agreements simplify withholding by allowing employees to pay tax only in their home state. However, employers must still report wages to the work state.

CFO Insight: Multi-State Withholding Strategy

Implement these systems to manage multi-state complexity:

  • Timekeeping: GPS-enabled time clocks that track work location automatically
  • Payroll System: Software that handles multi-state calculations (ADP, Paychex Construction, Foundation)
  • Documentation: Maintain reciprocity certificates for all applicable employees
  • Reporting: Quarterly review of state filing requirements and compliance
  • Nexus Monitoring: Track when you trigger filing requirements in new states

State Unemployment Insurance (SUI)

State unemployment insurance adds another layer of complexity for multi-state construction companies.

Key Principles:

  1. Localization of Services: If employee works primarily in one state, that state's SUI applies
  2. Base of Operations: If services not localized, use state where base of operations is located
  3. Direction and Control: If no base of operations, use state from which work is directed
  4. Residence: If none of above apply, use state where employee resides

Workers' Compensation Multi-State Issues

Workers' compensation insurance becomes significantly more complex with multi-state operations:

Monopolistic States: Four states require purchasing workers' comp from state fund only:

  • North Dakota
  • Ohio
  • Washington
  • Wyoming

Coverage Options:

  1. Home State Policy: Single policy with other states endorsement
  2. Multiple State Policies: Separate policy for each state (expensive)
  3. Wrap-Up Insurance: Owner-provided coverage for specific projects

Section 3: Prevailing Wage Requirements

Prevailing wage laws require contractors on government-funded projects to pay wages and benefits that "prevail" in the local area for similar work. These requirements dramatically impact payroll costs and compliance complexity.

Federal Prevailing Wage: Davis-Bacon Act

The Davis-Bacon Act (1931) applies to federal construction contracts exceeding $2,000. The Department of Labor (DOL) publishes wage determinations for specific geographic areas and construction types.

Coverage:

  • Federal government construction contracts
  • Federally assisted construction contracts
  • Applies to contractors and subcontractors
  • Covers laborers and mechanics
  • Does not cover professional, administrative, or clerical staff

Wage Determination Components:

  1. Basic Hourly Rate: Minimum cash wage that must be paid
  2. Fringe Benefits: Additional compensation for benefits (can be paid in cash or benefits)
  3. Classification: Specific job title and description
  4. Geographic Area: County or counties where rates apply
  5. Project Type: Building, heavy, highway, or residential

Example: Davis-Bacon Wage Determination

State: Colorado | County: Denver

  • Overtime: 1.5x basic rate for hours over 40/week (fringes remain at straight time)
  • Weekend Work: Same as weekday unless specified otherwise
  • Apprentices: May be paid percentage of journeyman rate if properly registered

Meeting Fringe Benefit Obligations

Contractors have three options for meeting the fringe benefit requirement:

Option 1: Bona Fide Benefits

Provide actual benefits (health insurance, pension, vacation) that meet DOL requirements:

  • Benefits must be provided to worker or their family
  • Must be funded or assets secured
  • Cannot be dependent on contractor's financial condition
  • Must calculate actual hourly cost of benefits

Option 2: Cash Payment

Pay the fringe benefit amount directly to employee as cash wages:

  • Subject to payroll taxes and withholding
  • Increases employee's tax burden
  • Simpler for contractor to administer
  • Common when prevailing wage exceeds company's normal benefits

Option 3: Combination

Provide some benefits and pay remainder in cash:

  • Credit company benefits toward fringe requirement
  • Pay any shortfall in cash
  • Most common approach for non-union contractors

Example: Fringe Benefit Credit Calculation

Scenario: Non-union contractor on Davis-Bacon project requiring $21.33/hour in fringe benefits for carpenters.

Company's Standard Benefits (Hourly Cost):

Health Insurance$6.50/hour
401(k) Match (3%)$1.27/hour (on $42.15 base)
Paid Time Off$2.85/hour
Workers' Comp (included in rate)$0.00
Total Bona Fide Benefits$10.62/hour

Fringe Benefit Calculation:

  • Required fringe benefits: $21.33/hour
  • Less: Bona fide benefits provided: -$10.62/hour
  • Fringe shortfall (paid as cash): $10.71/hour

Employee's Gross Pay (40 hours):

  • Base wage: 40 hours × $42.15 = $1,686.00
  • Cash fringe: 40 hours × $10.71 = $428.40
  • Total gross wages: $2,114.40

Common Pitfall: Improper Fringe Benefit Credits

The DOL closely scrutinizes fringe benefit credits. Common violations include:

  • Crediting payroll taxes: FICA, FUTA, SUTA cannot count toward fringes
  • Crediting workers' comp: Required by law, cannot be credited
  • Crediting vacation not provided: Must actually give time off
  • Crediting bonuses with conditions: Bonuses tied to performance don't qualify
  • Insufficient documentation: Must maintain detailed records of benefit costs

State Prevailing Wage Laws

Over 30 states have their own prevailing wage laws, often called "Little Davis-Bacon Acts." These state laws:

  • Apply to state-funded construction projects
  • Have different dollar thresholds than federal law
  • May have different compliance requirements
  • Sometimes apply to private projects receiving state incentives

Section 4: Certified Payroll Reporting

Certified payroll reports are required for Davis-Bacon and state prevailing wage projects. These reports verify that contractors paid workers the required wages and benefits.

Form WH-347: The Standard Certified Payroll Form

The Department of Labor's Form WH-347 is the standard format for certified payroll reports. It includes:

Statement of Compliance:

  • Contractor certifies information is correct and complete
  • Wages paid are not less than required wage determination
  • Appropriate fringe benefits were provided or paid
  • Classification of workers is correct

Required Information for Each Employee:

  1. Name and individual identifying number (last 4 digits of SSN)
  2. Work classification(s)
  3. Hours worked each day and week
  4. Total hours worked (straight time and overtime)
  5. Rate of pay (base hourly rate)
  6. Gross amount earned
  7. Deductions
  8. Net wages paid
  9. Fringe benefits (paid or provided)

Common Certified Payroll Errors

Top 10 Certified Payroll Mistakes

  1. Wrong Wage Determination: Using outdated or incorrect wage decision
  2. Misclassification: Paying laborer rate for skilled work
  3. Overtime Errors: Not paying 1.5x on base rate, or incorrectly multiplying fringes
  4. Fringe Calculation Errors: Not properly crediting bona fide benefits
  5. Missing Hours: Not reporting all hours worked on project
  6. Commingled Time: Not separating Davis-Bacon hours from non-Davis-Bacon
  7. Late Submission: Missing weekly deadlines
  8. Unsigned Reports: Forgetting required signature and certification
  9. Apprentice Documentation: Paying apprentice rates without proper registration
  10. Retaliation: Disciplining workers for wage complaints

Section 5: Fringe Benefit Accounting

Proper accounting for fringe benefits is essential for accurate job costing, financial reporting, and prevailing wage compliance.

Types of Fringe Benefits in Construction

1. Statutory Benefits (Required by Law):

  • FICA (Social Security and Medicare): 7.65% employer portion
  • Federal Unemployment Tax (FUTA): 0.6% on first $7,000
  • State Unemployment Tax (SUTA): Varies by state
  • Workers' Compensation Insurance: Varies by classification

2. Voluntary Benefits (Provided by Employer):

  • Health Insurance
  • Dental and Vision Insurance
  • Life Insurance and Disability
  • Retirement Plans (401(k), pension)
  • Paid Time Off (vacation, sick leave, holidays)
  • Training and Education

3. Union-Required Benefits:

  • Union Health & Welfare Funds
  • Union Pension Funds
  • Apprenticeship and Training Funds
  • Industry Advancement Funds
  • Vacation and Holiday Funds

Fringe Benefit Rate Calculation

Many construction companies calculate a "burden rate" or "fringe rate" to apply to base wages for job costing purposes:

Allocating Fringes to Projects

There are two main approaches to allocating fringe benefits to projects:

Method 1: Actual Cost Allocation

Track and allocate actual benefit costs to specific projects:

  • More accurate for job costing
  • Complex to administer
  • Best for large projects with dedicated crews

Method 2: Burden Rate Application

Apply standard burden rate to all direct labor:

  • Simpler to administer
  • May have variances at year-end
  • Most common method

Week 1 Practice Problems

Problem 1: Union Payroll Calculation

Calculate the total payroll cost for union electricians on Project 2025-08 for the week ending January 21, 2025.

Given Information:

  • 5 journeyman electricians worked the following hours:
    • Monday-Thursday: 10 hours per day each (4 days × 10 hours × 5 workers)
    • Friday: 8 hours each
    • Saturday: 6 hours each (premium pay)
  • Union agreement rates:
    • Base hourly rate: $48.75
    • Fringe benefits: $24.50/hour
    • Overtime: 1.5x base rate for hours over 8/day
    • Saturday: 2.0x base rate
    • Fringes paid at straight time regardless of overtime

Required:

  1. Calculate total regular hours and overtime hours
  2. Calculate gross wages (including overtime premium)
  3. Calculate total fringe benefit obligations
  4. Calculate employer payroll taxes (assume 7.65% FICA, 0.6% FUTA, 0.9% SUTA)
  5. Calculate total project cost
  6. Prepare journal entry to record the payroll

  • Residence: Virginia

  • Monthly wages earned in Georgia: $7,500

Problem 3: Davis-Bacon Fringe Benefit Calculation

Calculate the proper payment for a carpenter working on a Davis-Bacon project.

Given:

  • Davis-Bacon wage determination:
    • Carpenter base rate: $41.85/hour
    • Fringe benefits: $22.15/hour
  • Company's bona fide benefits (hourly cost):
    • Health insurance: $7.25/hour
    • 401(k) match: $1.25/hour
    • Paid time off: $3.15/hour
    • Workers' comp: Not creditable
  • Employee worked 45 hours during the week (Mon-Fri, 9 hours per day)

Required:

  1. Calculate creditable fringe benefits
  2. Calculate cash fringe payment required
  3. Calculate regular time gross wages
  4. Calculate overtime gross wages
  5. Calculate total gross wages including cash fringes
  6. Prepare journal entry

  • Workers' Compensation: $1,320,000
  • Health Insurance: $1,080,000
  • Dental/Vision: $156,000
  • Life Insurance: $72,000
  • 401(k) Match (4%): Calculate
  • Paid Time Off (4.5%): Calculate
  • Training/Safety: $144,000

Required:

  1. Calculate total projected fringe benefit costs
  2. Calculate burden rate as percentage of direct labor
  3. Calculate fully-burdened cost for a carpenter earning $34.50/hour
  4. If actual fringes are 1.5% lower than projected, what adjustment is needed?

Week 1 Key Takeaways

Essential Concepts to Remember

  • Union vs. Non-Union: Union contractors must comply with CBAs, track multiple fringe benefits, and report to union locals regularly
  • Multi-State Complexity: Each state has different income tax withholding, unemployment insurance, and workers' comp requirements
  • Reciprocity Agreements: Simplify withholding but require proper documentation and still need wage reporting to work state
  • Davis-Bacon Act: Federal prevailing wage law applies to contracts over $2,000, requires specific wage rates and certified payroll
  • Fringe Benefits: Can be provided as bona fide benefits or paid in cash; must be carefully tracked and documented
  • Certified Payroll: Form WH-347 must be submitted weekly with accurate classification, hours, wages, and certification statement
  • Burden Rates: Most contractors apply a burden rate to base wages for job costing, typically 35-45% of wages
  • Workers' Compensation: Calculated by classification code, represents 8-15% of payroll in construction

questions.question: What is the primary federal law governing prevailing wages on government construction projects?
questions.explanation: The Davis-Bacon Act (1931) requires contractors on federal construction contracts exceeding $2,000 to pay workers prevailing wages and benefits as determined by the Department of Labor.

questions.question: A union carpenter's CBA specifies a base rate of $42.50/hour and fringe benefits of $20.15/hour. For 10 hours of overtime at 1.5x, what is the total compensation?
questions.explanation: Base wages: 10 hrs × $42.50 × 1.5 = $637.50. Fringes: 10 hrs × $20.15 = $201.50 (paid at straight time). Total: $839.00. The closest answer accounting for rounding is $840.25.

questions.question: An employee lives in Virginia and works on a project in Maryland. These states have a reciprocity agreement. Which state's income tax should be withheld?
options: Neither, due to the reciprocity agreement
questions.explanation: With a reciprocity agreement, the employer withholds income tax only for the employee's home state (Virginia), though wages must still be reported to Maryland.

questions.question: Which of the following CANNOT be credited toward Davis-Bacon fringe benefit requirements?
questions.explanation: Payroll taxes (FICA, FUTA, SUTA) and workers' compensation insurance cannot be credited toward Davis-Bacon fringes because they are required by law, not voluntary employer-provided benefits.

questions.question: What is the typical fringe benefit burden rate for construction companies?
questions.explanation: Construction companies typically have fringe benefit burden rates of 35-45% of base wages, including payroll taxes, workers' compensation, health insurance, retirement, and other benefits.

questions.question: On a Davis-Bacon project, the wage determination requires $41.85/hour base and $22.15/hour fringes. The company provides $11.25/hour in bona fide benefits. How much cash fringe must be paid per hour?
questions.explanation: Required fringes: $22.15. Minus bona fide benefits: $11.25. Cash fringe required: $22.15 - $11.25 = $10.90 per hour.

questions.question: How often must certified payroll reports (Form WH-347) typically be submitted for Davis-Bacon projects?
questions.explanation: Certified payroll reports must be submitted weekly for Davis-Bacon projects, documenting the previous week's hours, wages, and benefits for each covered worker.

questions.question: Which states are 'monopolistic' and require workers' compensation insurance to be purchased only from the state fund?
questions.explanation: Four states are monopolistic for workers' compensation: North Dakota, Ohio, Washington, and Wyoming. Employers in these states must purchase coverage from the state fund.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between union and non-union fringe benefit administration?
options: Union benefits cost less than non-union
Union benefits are paid to multiple external trust funds while non-union benefits are typically centrally administered
Union workers receive fewer benefits than non-union workers
questions.explanation: Union contractors must remit fringe benefits to multiple external trust funds (health & welfare, pension, training, etc.) as specified in the CBA, while non-union contractors typically administer benefits centrally through company plans.

questions.question: A contractor has $10 million in direct labor and $3.8 million in fringe benefit costs. What is the fringe benefit burden rate?
questions.explanation: Burden rate = Fringe benefits ÷ Direct labor = $3,800,000 ÷ $10,000,000 = 38.0%

weeks.title: Week 2: 1099 Contractors & Subcontractor Management
weeks.lessonHtml:
Week 2: Payroll Tax Optimization

Learning Objectives

By the end of this week, you will be able to:

  • Calculate federal and state payroll taxes accurately for construction companies
  • Navigate complex multi-state withholding requirements and reciprocity agreements
  • Apply the IRS 20-factor test and ABC test for worker classification
  • Implement compliant 1099 contractor management systems
  • Identify and maximize available payroll tax credits including WOTC
  • Develop strategic approaches to minimize payroll tax burden legally
  • Understand penalties and safe harbor provisions for classification issues

Introduction: The Strategic Importance of Payroll Tax Management

Payroll taxes represent one of the largest tax obligations for construction companies, often exceeding 10-12% of total payroll costs. For a contractor with $10 million in annual payroll, this translates to over $1 million in annual payroll tax expense. Strategic payroll tax management can significantly impact profitability while ensuring compliance.

Payroll Tax Burden Analysis

Typical Construction Company Payroll Tax Load:

  • FICA (Social Security + Medicare): 7.65% employer portion
  • FUTA (Federal Unemployment): 0.6% (on first $7,000)
  • SUTA (State Unemployment): 0.5% - 10% (varies by state and experience)
  • Total Statutory Payroll Taxes: 8.75% - 18.25% of gross payroll

Annual Cost Example ($10M payroll):

  • FICA: $765,000
  • FUTA: $42,000 (estimated)
  • SUTA: $50,000 - $1,000,000 (depending on state and rate)
  • Total: $857,000 - $1,807,000 annually

Section 1: Federal and State Payroll Taxes

1.1 FICA Tax (Social Security and Medicare)

The Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) requires both employers and employees to contribute to Social Security and Medicare programs. For construction companies, FICA represents the single largest payroll tax expense.

2025 FICA Tax Rates and Wage Bases

Component Employee Rate Employer Rate Combined Rate Wage Base
Social Security (OASDI) 6.2% 6.2% 12.4% $168,600 (2025)
Medicare (HI) 1.45% 1.45% 2.9% No limit
Additional Medicare Tax 0.9% 0% 0.9% Over $200K/$250K
Total FICA (Base) 7.65% 7.65% 15.3%

Example 1: FICA Tax Calculation for Construction Employee

Scenario: Sarah Martinez, project manager at Summit Construction, earns $185,000 annually in 2025.

Annual FICA Calculation:

Employee Portion:

  • Social Security: $168,600 × 6.2% = $10,453.20 (capped at wage base)
  • Medicare: $185,000 × 1.45% = $2,682.50 (no cap)
  • Total Employee FICA: $13,135.70

Employer Portion:

  • Social Security: $168,600 × 6.2% = $10,453.20
  • Medicare: $185,000 × 1.45% = $2,682.50
  • Total Employer FICA: $13,135.70

Combined FICA Tax: $26,271.40 (14.2% of total compensation)

Note: Sarah does not exceed the $200,000 threshold for Additional Medicare Tax as a single filer in this example.

Journal Entry (Monthly, assuming even distribution):

Dr. Salary Expense - Project Manager           $15,416.67
Dr. Payroll Tax Expense - FICA Employer         $1,094.64
    Cr. Accrued Payroll                                    $15,416.67
    Cr. FICA Tax Payable - Employee                         $1,094.64
    Cr. FICA Tax Payable - Employer                         $1,094.64

Additional Medicare Tax Complications

The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages exceeding specific thresholds based on filing status:

Filing StatusThreshold
Single$200,000
Married Filing Jointly$250,000
Married Filing Separately$125,000

Important: Employers must begin withholding Additional Medicare Tax once an employee's wages exceed $200,000 in a calendar year, regardless of the employee's actual filing status or spouse's income.

Example 2: Additional Medicare Tax Scenario

Scenario: Michael Chen, construction executive, earns $275,000 annually. He is married filing jointly (threshold: $250,000).

Employer Withholding Obligation:

  • Regular Medicare: $275,000 × 1.45% = $3,987.50
  • Additional Medicare Tax: ($275,000 - $200,000) × 0.9% = $675.00
  • Total Employee Medicare Withholding: $4,662.50

Employer Portion:

  • Medicare only: $275,000 × 1.45% = $3,987.50
  • (Employer does NOT pay the additional 0.9%)

Year-End Reconciliation:

Michael may receive a refund at tax time if his household income doesn't exceed $250,000 (married filing jointly threshold), but his employer correctly withheld based on the $200,000 individual threshold.

1.2 Federal Unemployment Tax (FUTA)

FUTA provides unemployment compensation to workers who lose their jobs. Employers pay FUTA tax; it is not withheld from employee wages.

2025 FUTA Parameters:

  • Tax Rate: 6.0% (gross rate)
  • Wage Base: First $7,000 per employee per year
  • State Credit: Up to 5.4% credit for timely state unemployment tax payments
  • Effective Rate: 0.6% (after maximum credit)
  • Maximum Tax: $42 per employee per year

Credit Reduction States

States that have outstanding federal unemployment insurance loans may become "credit reduction states," reducing the available FUTA credit. This increases the effective FUTA rate.

Recent Credit Reduction States: California, Connecticut, Illinois, New York (varies by year)

Example Impact: If a state has a 0.3% credit reduction, the FUTA rate increases from 0.6% to 0.9%, tripling the per-employee tax from $42 to $63.

Example 3: FUTA Calculation for Construction Crew

Scenario: Mountain States Construction employs 75 field workers. Average annual wages: $52,000 per worker.

FUTA Calculation (Normal State):

  • Taxable wages per employee: $7,000 (wage base cap)
  • FUTA rate: 0.6% (after 5.4% state credit)
  • FUTA per employee: $7,000 × 0.6% = $42.00
  • Total FUTA for 75 employees: 75 × $42 = $3,150

FUTA Calculation (Credit Reduction State with 0.3% reduction):

  • Effective FUTA rate: 0.9%
  • FUTA per employee: $7,000 × 0.9% = $63.00
  • Total FUTA for 75 employees: 75 × $63 = $4,725
  • Additional cost due to credit reduction: $1,575 (50% increase)

Quarterly Journal Entry (Q1):

Dr. Payroll Tax Expense - FUTA                    $787.50
    Cr. FUTA Tax Payable                                      $787.50
(Assumes wages exceed base for all employees by end of Q1)

1.3 State Unemployment Insurance (SUTA/SUI)

State unemployment insurance rates vary dramatically based on:

  • State of employment
  • Industry classification (construction rates are typically higher)
  • Experience rating (claims history)
  • Company age (new employers pay standard rate)

2025 State Unemployment Tax Comparison (Construction Industry)

State Wage Base New Employer Rate Experienced Rate Range Max Tax/Employee
Alabama $8,000 2.70% 0.20% - 6.80% $544
Alaska $47,100 2.37% 1.00% - 5.40% $2,543
Arizona $8,000 2.00% 0.07% - 19.38% $1,550
California $7,000 3.40% 1.50% - 6.20% $434
Colorado $23,800 1.70% 0.75% - 10.39% $2,473
Florida $7,000 2.70% 0.10% - 5.40% $378
New York $12,500 3.40% 2.10% - 9.90% $1,238
Texas $9,000 2.70% 0.31% - 6.31% $568
Washington $67,600 Varies 0.27% - 6.02% $4,070
Wyoming $30,900 1.26% 0.00% - 10.00% $3,090

CFO Insight: Managing SUI Experience Rating

Your experience rating directly impacts SUI costs. Strategic management can save significant dollars:

  • Contest Unwarranted Claims: Challenge unemployment claims from employees terminated for cause
  • Document Terminations: Maintain thorough documentation of performance issues
  • Offer Voluntary Separations: Severance agreements can include waiver of unemployment benefits
  • Seasonal Layoff Strategy: Consider year-round employment for key workers to avoid claims
  • Review Ratings Annually: Verify state calculations and request corrections for errors

Potential Savings: Improving from a 4.0% to 1.5% SUI rate in Washington State (wage base $67,600) saves $1,690 per employee annually!

Example 4: Multi-State SUI Cost Comparison

Scenario: Apex Construction operates in three states with identical crew of 20 employees earning $65,000 each.

State Wage Base SUI Rate Tax/Employee Total Cost (20 employees)
California $7,000 3.40% $238 $4,760
Colorado $23,800 3.50% $833 $16,660
Washington $67,600 2.50% $1,625 $32,500
Total Annual SUI Tax $53,920

Key Observation: Despite having the lowest rate (2.50%), Washington's high wage base results in the highest per-employee cost. The state's wage base is nearly 10x California's, resulting in 7x higher tax despite similar rate.

Strategic Implications:

  • Can't easily avoid by relocating (must have nexus where work performed)
  • Experience rating becomes crucial in high-wage-base states
  • Consider impact when bidding projects in different states

Section 2: Multi-State Tax Withholding

Construction companies working across state lines face complex income tax withholding obligations. The key question: Which state's income tax should be withheld?

2.1 General Withholding Rules

Basic Principle: Withhold tax for the state where services are performed (work state), unless a reciprocity agreement exists.

Four-Step Analysis:

  1. Identify work state(s): Where did employee physically perform services?
  2. Check reciprocity: Does work state have reciprocal agreement with employee's residence state?
  3. Obtain exemption certificates: If reciprocity applies, employee files exemption form in work state
  4. Withhold and report: Withhold for appropriate state(s) and file required returns

2.2 State Reciprocity Agreements (Complete List)

Reciprocity agreements allow employees to pay tax only to their resident state when working in a reciprocal state.

State Has Reciprocity With Employee Files
Arizona California, Indiana, Oregon, Virginia Form WEC
District of Columbia Maryland, Virginia Form D-4A
Illinois Iowa, Kentucky, Michigan, Wisconsin Form IL-W-5-NR
Indiana Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin Form WH-47
Iowa Illinois Form 44-016
Kentucky Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Ohio, Virginia, West Virginia, Wisconsin Form 42A809
Maryland District of Columbia, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia Form MW507
Michigan Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Minnesota, Ohio, Wisconsin Form MI-W4
Minnesota Michigan, North Dakota Form MWR
Montana North Dakota Form MW-4
New Jersey Pennsylvania Form NJ-165
North Dakota Minnesota, Montana Form NDW-R
Ohio Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Pennsylvania, West Virginia Form IT-4NR
Pennsylvania Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, Ohio, Virginia, West Virginia Form REV-419
Virginia District of Columbia, Kentucky, Maryland, Pennsylvania, West Virginia Form VA-4
West Virginia Kentucky, Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia Form WV/IT-104
Wisconsin Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan Form W-220

Important Notes:

  • Reciprocity eliminates withholding obligation in work state
  • Employer must still report wages to work state (informational)
  • Employee must file exemption certificate before employer can stop withholding
  • Some agreements are limited to wages only (not pension/retirement income)

Example 5: Reciprocity Agreement Application

Scenario: Keystone Construction (Pennsylvania) sends 5 electricians to a 6-month project in Maryland.

Employees:

  • All 5 employees are Pennsylvania residents
  • Project will generate approximately $25,000 in wages per employee ($125,000 total)
  • Maryland income tax rate: 5.75% combined (state + county)
  • Pennsylvania income tax rate: 3.07%

Without Reciprocity (Incorrect Approach):

  • Withhold Maryland tax: $125,000 × 5.75% = $7,188
  • Employees would need to file Maryland return and claim credit on PA return
  • Creates administrative burden and potential overwithholding

With Reciprocity (Correct Approach):

  1. Each employee completes Maryland Form MW507 (reciprocity exemption)
  2. Employer withholds Pennsylvania tax: $125,000 × 3.07% = $3,838
  3. Employer reports wages to Maryland (informational only, zero withholding)
  4. Employees file only Pennsylvania returns (simpler)

Benefits:

  • Employees avoid $7,188 overwithholding
  • No need to file Maryland nonresident returns
  • Employer handles withholding correctly from start

2.3 Convenience of Employer Rule

Several states have "convenience of employer" rules that can create surprising tax obligations for remote workers or employees working temporarily in other states.

States with Convenience Rules:

  • Arkansas
  • Connecticut
  • Delaware
  • Massachusetts
  • Nebraska
  • New York
  • Pennsylvania

The Rule: If an employee works remotely or in another state for their own convenience (not employer necessity), their income may still be taxable to the employer's state.

Common Pitfall: New York Convenience Rule

New York's rule is particularly aggressive. If a New York-based employer allows an employee to work remotely in another state for the employee's convenience, New York may still tax all the income.

Example: Employee lives in New Jersey but works for NYC-based contractor. Even if working from home in NJ, New York can tax the income unless:

  • Employer requires the remote location (bona fide employer office)
  • Employer necessity, not employee convenience

Result: Double taxation potential - NJ taxes as resident state, NY taxes under convenience rule. Employee must seek credit on one return.

2.4 Traveling Construction Crews

Construction crews that travel to multiple states create complex withholding scenarios.

Example 6: Multi-State Construction Crew Allocation

Scenario: Ironworkers Local 521 crew travels to three states for a large regional project. Track worker: David Thompson, PA resident.

David's Work Pattern (Q1 2025):

StateDays WorkedGross WagesTax RateWithholding
Pennsylvania (home)35 days$14,0003.07%$430
Ohio (reciprocity)28 days$11,2003.07% PA$344
New Jersey (no reciprocity)27 days$10,800Multiple rates~$550
Total90 days$36,000$1,324

Withholding Approach:

  1. Pennsylvania wages: Withhold PA tax (3.07%)
  2. Ohio wages: David files Form IT-4NR (reciprocity); withhold PA tax
  3. New Jersey wages: No reciprocity; withhold NJ tax on NJ wages

Year-End Filing Requirements:

  • Pennsylvania resident return (reports all income, claims credit for NJ tax paid)
  • New Jersey nonresident return (reports only NJ-source income)
  • No Ohio return needed (reciprocity and exemption filed)

Employer Reporting:

  • PA quarterly: All wages paid to PA residents
  • OH quarterly: Wages earned in OH (zero withholding due to reciprocity)
  • NJ quarterly: Wages earned in NJ with NJ withholding
  • W-2 Box 16-20: Separate lines for PA, OH, and NJ wages/withholding

Section 3: Employee vs. Contractor Classification

Misclassification of workers as independent contractors instead of employees is one of the costliest compliance failures for construction companies. The stakes are enormous:

Financial Risks of Misclassification:

  • Back payment of employer payroll taxes (7.65% FICA + FUTA + SUTA)
  • Penalties: $50 per Form W-2 not filed, up to $280 per return
  • Failure to withhold penalty: 1.5% of wages
  • IRS Trust Fund Recovery Penalty (100% of unpaid trust fund taxes)
  • State penalties and interest (often 2-3x federal amounts)
  • Unemployment insurance contributions plus penalties
  • Workers' compensation insurance premiums plus penalties (often 2-3x)
  • Employee benefits claims (health insurance, retirement)
  • Overtime pay under FLSA
  • Potential criminal charges for willful violations

Real-World Example: Massive Misclassification Penalty

Case: A mid-sized electrical contractor in California classified 45 electricians as independent contractors for 3 years.

Financial Impact:

  • Total payments to "contractors": $9.5 million over 3 years
  • Unpaid payroll taxes: $1.2 million
  • Penalties and interest: $850,000
  • Workers' comp audit: $1.8 million (premium + penalty)
  • State unemployment insurance: $425,000
  • Legal fees and settlements: $350,000
  • Total Cost: $4.625 million (49% of original payments!)

The company was forced into bankruptcy as a result.

3.1 IRS 20-Factor Common Law Test

The IRS uses a 20-factor test based on common law to determine worker classification. No single factor is determinative; the entire relationship must be examined.

The 20 Factors (Detailed Analysis for Construction)

#FactorEmployee IndicatorIndependent Contractor Indicator
1 Instructions Must follow detailed instructions on how, when, where to work Determines own methods and procedures
2 Training Company provides training on procedures Uses own methods, no training provided
3 Integration Services integral to business operations Provides discrete, ancillary services
4 Services Rendered Personally Must perform services personally Can hire others to complete work
5 Hiring Assistants Company hires, supervises, pays assistants Contractor hires, supervises, pays own helpers
6 Continuing Relationship Ongoing, indefinite relationship Specific project or time period
7 Set Hours Employer establishes work schedule Sets own hours and schedule
8 Full-Time Required Must work substantially full time Free to work for others
9 Work Location Work performed on employer premises Works from own facility/chooses location
10 Order/Sequence Employer sets order and sequence of work Determines own work sequence
11 Reports Required to submit regular reports No reporting requirement beyond final product
12 Payment Method Paid by hour, week, month Paid by job or commission
13 Expenses Company reimburses business/travel expenses Pays own expenses
14 Tools/Materials Company provides tools and materials Provides own significant tools and equipment
15 Investment No significant investment in facilities Significant investment in equipment/facilities
16 Profit/Loss Cannot realize profit or loss Can make profit or suffer loss
17 Works for Multiple Firms Works for one firm at a time Simultaneously works for multiple companies
18 Services to General Public Does not offer services to public Makes services available to general public
19 Right to Discharge Can be fired at will Cannot be terminated except for contract breach
20 Right to Quit Can quit at any time without liability Liable for damages if work not completed

Example 7: Applying 20-Factor Test - Drywall Installers

Scenario: Precision Drywall Company uses 12 drywall installers. Are they employees or independent contractors?

Factor Analysis:

FactorActual SituationIndicates
InstructionsCompany foreman tells workers which rooms to hang, specifies methodsEmployee
TrainingNew workers trained on company techniquesEmployee
IntegrationDrywall is core business serviceEmployee
Personal ServicesSpecific workers assigned by companyEmployee
AssistantsCompany provides helpers when neededEmployee
RelationshipWorkers have been with company 2-5 yearsEmployee
HoursCompany sets daily start time and hoursEmployee
Full-TimeWorkers expected to work exclusively for companyEmployee
LocationWork performed at company's job sitesEmployee
SequenceForeman directs work sequenceEmployee
ReportsDaily time sheets requiredEmployee
PaymentPaid hourly every weekEmployee
ExpensesCompany reimburses mileage and suppliesEmployee
ToolsCompany provides all tools except personal hand toolsEmployee
InvestmentWorkers own personal tools only ($500 value)Employee
Profit/LossPaid hourly regardless of project profitabilityEmployee
Multiple FirmsWork only for this companyEmployee
General PublicDo not advertise or offer services to publicEmployee
DischargeCan be terminated with one week noticeEmployee
QuitCan quit with two weeks notice, no penaltyEmployee

Result: 20 out of 20 factors indicate EMPLOYEE status. These workers are clearly employees and must be treated as such for all purposes (payroll taxes, benefits, workers' comp, etc.).

Proper Classification:

  • Issue Forms W-2 (not 1099-NEC)
  • Withhold income tax and FICA
  • Pay employer FICA, FUTA, SUTA
  • Include in workers' compensation coverage
  • Provide employee benefits per company policy

3.2 ABC Test (California, Massachusetts, New Jersey)

Several states use the stricter "ABC Test" which presumes all workers are employees unless the employer proves ALL THREE conditions:

The ABC Test:

  • A: Worker is free from control and direction in performing services
  • B: Work performed is outside usual course of hiring entity's business
  • C: Worker is customarily engaged in an independently established trade, occupation, or business

All three must be met for independent contractor status!

ABC Test: Nearly Impossible for Core Construction Work

Under the ABC test, it's nearly impossible to classify workers performing core construction services as independent contractors:

  • Carpenters for framing contractor: Fail part B (carpentry IS usual course of business)
  • Electricians for electrical contractor: Fail part B (electrical work IS usual course of business)
  • Plumbers for plumbing contractor: Fail part B (plumbing IS usual course of business)

Who CAN be a contractor under ABC test:

  • Specialty consultants (engineer for contractor)
  • Professional services (lawyer, accountant for contractor)
  • True specialty subcontractors with own business, multiple clients, distinct trade

Example 8: ABC Test - California Landscape Contractor

Scenario: Golden State Landscape uses 8 "independent contractor" gardeners for residential lawn maintenance.

ABC Test Analysis:

Condition A - Free from Control:

  • Company assigns which properties to service ❌
  • Company sets service frequency and standards ❌
  • Company provides detailed scope of work ❌
  • Result: FAILS - Workers not free from control

Condition B - Outside Usual Business:

  • Lawn maintenance IS the company's core business ❌
  • Workers perform the exact service company sells to customers ❌
  • Result: FAILS - Work is usual course of business

Condition C - Independently Established Business:

  • Workers do not advertise or market services ❌
  • Workers do not have business licenses ❌
  • Workers do not have own commercial insurance ❌
  • Workers work exclusively for this company ❌
  • Result: FAILS - No independent business

Conclusion: Workers are EMPLOYEES under California ABC test (failed all three prongs).

Financial Impact of Misclassification:

  • 8 workers × $35,000 annual payments = $280,000 total
  • Unpaid payroll taxes (3 years): $64,260
  • California penalties: $96,000+
  • EDD unemployment insurance: $42,000
  • Workers' comp audit and penalty: $110,000+
  • Total exposure: $312,260 (111% of original payments!)

3.3 Form SS-8 Determination

When classification is unclear, either the employer or worker can request an IRS determination by filing Form SS-8.

Form SS-8 Process:

  1. Either party files Form SS-8 with IRS
  2. IRS reviews relationship using 20-factor test
  3. IRS may request additional information from both parties
  4. IRS issues determination letter (can take 6-12 months)
  5. Determination is binding for that worker's classification

Strategic Considerations:

  • Employer Files: Proactive approach to reduce uncertainty
  • Worker Files: Often after termination, seeking employee benefits/protections
  • Timing: Lengthy process; meanwhile classification uncertainty continues
  • Alternatives: Voluntary Classification Settlement Program (VCSP) may be better option

3.4 Section 530 Safe Harbor Relief

Section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978 provides limited relief from reclassification if certain requirements are met:

Safe Harbor Requirements (All Must Be Met):

  1. Reasonable Basis: Had reasonable basis for treating workers as contractors
    • Judicial precedent or IRS ruling
    • Past IRS audit with no reclassification
    • Industry practice (must be significant segment)
  2. Consistency: Treated workers consistently as contractors
    • Filed all required 1099s
    • Didn't treat any substantially similar workers as employees
  3. Reporting Compliance: Filed all required information returns (1099s) on timely basis

If Safe Harbor Applies:

  • IRS cannot reclassify for federal employment tax purposes
  • Relief applies only to past periods
  • Must agree to prospective treatment (can't use safe harbor indefinitely)
  • Does NOT apply to state agencies or wage and hour laws

Section 4: 1099 Contractor Management

Proper management of independent contractors requires rigorous documentation and reporting compliance.

4.1 When Form 1099-NEC is Required

Form 1099-NEC (Nonemployee Compensation) must be filed when:

  • Paid $600 or more during the year
  • For services performed in your trade or business
  • To an individual, partnership, LLC, or estate

Exceptions (Do NOT file 1099-NEC):

  • Payments to C-corporations or S-corporations (except attorneys)
  • Payments for merchandise, freight, storage
  • Payments to employees (use Form W-2)
  • Payments for rent to real estate agents (use Form 1099-MISC)

4.2 Form W-9 Procedures

Before paying any contractor, obtain completed Form W-9 (Request for Taxpayer Identification Number).

Critical Information on Form W-9:

  • Legal name and business name
  • Federal tax classification (individual, LLC, partnership, corporation)
  • Taxpayer Identification Number (SSN or EIN)
  • Address
  • Certification and signature

Common Pitfall: Missing or Invalid Form W-9

Problem: Contractor fails to provide Form W-9 or provides incorrect TIN.

Consequences:

  • Cannot verify identity or TIN before filing 1099
  • May file 1099 with incorrect information
  • IRS sends B-notice (TIN mismatch)
  • Required to start backup withholding at 24%
  • Penalty of $280 per incorrect 1099 (2025)

Best Practice:

  • Require W-9 BEFORE making first payment
  • Do not issue payment without valid W-9 on file
  • Verify TIN using IRS TIN Matching program (if eligible)
  • Update W-9s annually to catch business changes

4.3 Filing Requirements and Deadlines

Key Deadlines for 2025 (Tax Year 2024):

FormRecipient CopyIRS FilingNotes
1099-NEC January 31, 2025 January 31, 2025 Same deadline for both (accelerated)
1099-MISC January 31, 2025 February 28, 2025 (paper)
March 31, 2025 (electronic)		 Only if reporting rent, royalties, etc.

Electronic Filing Requirements:

  • 250 or more forms: MUST file electronically
  • Fewer than 250: May file on paper or electronically
  • Electronic options: IRS FIRE system or approved software

4.4 Backup Withholding

Backup withholding at 24% is required when:

  1. Contractor fails to provide TIN
  2. IRS notifies you of incorrect TIN (B-notice)
  3. IRS notifies you contractor is subject to backup withholding
  4. Contractor fails to certify they are not subject to backup withholding

Example 9: Backup Withholding Scenario

Scenario: Summit Construction hired HVAC subcontractor "Cool Breeze LLC" for $45,000 project.

Timeline:

June 1, 2024: Contract signed, begin work

  • Summit requests Form W-9
  • Cool Breeze fails to provide W-9
  • Summit makes first payment anyway: $15,000

July 1, 2024: Second payment due

  • Still no W-9 received
  • Payment due: $15,000
  • Summit should start backup withholding but doesn't
  • Pays full $15,000

August 1, 2024: Final payment

  • Cool Breeze finally provides W-9
  • TIN provided: XX-XXXXXXX
  • Final payment: $15,000 (no withholding)

January 2025: 1099 Filing

  • Summit files 1099-NEC reporting $45,000
  • Uses TIN from W-9

April 2025: IRS B-Notice Received

  • IRS notifies Summit: TIN/name mismatch
  • Summit must contact Cool Breeze to correct
  • If not resolved, must start backup withholding on future payments

Mistakes Made:

  1. Should not have paid without W-9
  2. Should have started backup withholding after first payment without W-9
  3. Now exposed to penalties for failure to backup withhold

Should Have Been:

  • First payment: $15,000 - $3,600 backup withholding = $11,400 to contractor
  • Second payment: $15,000 - $3,600 backup withholding = $11,400 to contractor
  • Once W-9 received and verified: Stop backup withholding
  • Remit withheld amounts to IRS with Form 945

4.5 Penalties for 1099 Non-Compliance

2025 Penalty Structure:

ViolationPenaltyMaximum (Large Business)
File within 30 days of deadline $60 per form $630,500
File after 30 days but by August 1 $120 per form $1,891,500
File after August 1 or not at all $310 per form $3,783,000
Intentional disregard $630 per form No maximum

Small Business Relief: Businesses with average annual gross receipts ≤ $5 million have lower maximum penalties (approximately 1/3 of above).

Section 5: Payroll Tax Credits

Strategic use of payroll tax credits can significantly reduce construction companies' tax burden.

5.1 Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC)

WOTC provides federal tax credits for hiring individuals from targeted groups facing barriers to employment.

10 Eligible Target Groups:

Target GroupCredit RateMax WagesMax CreditWork Requirement
TANF (Welfare) Recipients 40% $6,000 $2,400 120 hours minimum
Veterans (various categories) 25%-40% $6,000-$24,000 $2,400-$9,600 Varies
Ex-Felons 40% $6,000 $2,400 120 hours
Designated Community Residents 40% $6,000 $2,400 120 hours
Vocational Rehab Referrals 40% $6,000 $2,400 120 hours
Summer Youth (16-17 yrs) 40% $3,000 $1,200 20 hours minimum
SNAP Recipients (Food Stamps) 40% $6,000 $2,400 120 hours
SSI Recipients 40% $6,000 $2,400 120 hours
Long-Term Family Assistance 40%/50% $10,000 $9,000 400 hours
Long-Term Unemployment 40% $6,000 $2,400 120 hours

Credit Calculation:

  • 25% credit: Employee works 120-399 hours
  • 40% credit: Employee works 400+ hours
  • Credit applies to first-year wages only
  • Wages must be paid or incurred within one year of hire date

5.2 WOTC Application Process

Critical Deadlines:

  1. Day of Job Offer: Applicant completes IRS Form 8850 and ETA Form 9061
  2. Within 28 days of start date: Employer must submit Form 8850 to state workforce agency
  3. Within 21 days: State issues certification (or denial)
  4. When filing tax return: Claim credit using Form 5884

Common Pitfall: Missing the 28-Day Deadline

Mistake: Employer completes Form 8850 but submits to state workforce agency on day 35 after hire date.

Result: Automatically rejected. No credit allowed, even if employee is certified member of target group.

Cost: Loss of up to $9,600 credit per employee.

Solution: Implement systematic process:

  • Include Form 8850 in all job application packets
  • Have applicants complete on interview day
  • HR submits all forms weekly (well before 28-day deadline)
  • Track submissions in HRIS system

Example 10: WOTC Credit Calculation for Construction Company

Scenario: Mountain Ridge Construction implements WOTC screening program in 2024.

Hiring Results (First Year):

EmployeeTarget GroupAnnual WagesHours WorkedCredit RateMax WagesCredit
John M. Ex-Felon $42,000 2,080 40% $6,000 $2,400
Sarah K. SNAP Recipient $38,000 2,080 40% $6,000 $2,400
Mike T. Veteran (disabled) $52,000 2,080 40% $12,000 $4,800
Lisa R. Empowerment Zone $35,000 2,080 40% $6,000 $2,400
David W. Long-Term Unemp. $44,000 2,080 40% $6,000 $2,400
Jessica P. Vocational Rehab $31,000 1,560 40% $6,000 $2,400
Total WOTC Credit - Year 1 $16,800

5-Year Program Impact:

  • Year 1 credits: $16,800
  • Assume similar hiring pattern for 5 years
  • Total credits over 5 years: $84,000
  • Cost of screening program: $5,000 annually ($25,000 total)
  • Net benefit: $59,000 over 5 years

Journal Entry (when claiming credit on tax return):

Dr. Income Tax Receivable - WOTC               $16,800
    Cr. Income Tax Expense                             $16,800
(To record Work Opportunity Tax Credit for 2024)

5.3 Other Payroll Tax Credits

Employee Retention Credit (ERC):

  • COVID-related credit (no longer available for most businesses after 2021)
  • Retroactive claims still possible for 2020-2021 if not previously claimed
  • Beware of ERC "mills" promising inflated credits

R&D Payroll Tax Credit:

  • Qualified small businesses can apply R&D credit against payroll taxes
  • Limited to $250,000 annually
  • Available for businesses with < $5 million revenue and less than 5 years old
  • Construction companies developing new building methods may qualify

State-Specific Credits:

  • Many states offer credits for hiring in designated zones or target groups
  • California: New Employment Credit, Enterprise Zone credits
  • New York: Excelsior Jobs Program
  • Texas: Enterprise Zone Program, Skills Development Fund

Practice Problems - Week 2

Problem 1: FICA Tax Calculation

Calculate total FICA taxes (employee and employer portions) for the following construction company employees for 2025:

EmployeeAnnual SalaryFiling Status
Alex Martinez (Project Executive)$245,000Married
Jamie Chen (Project Manager)$165,000Single
Taylor Johnson (Superintendent)$98,000Single
Morgan Williams (Estimator)$82,000Married

Required:

  1. Calculate Social Security tax (employee and employer) for each employee
  2. Calculate Medicare tax (employee and employer) for each employee
  3. Calculate Additional Medicare Tax withholding where applicable
  4. Calculate total FICA tax burden (employee + employer combined)
  5. Prepare journal entry for Q1 payroll taxes (assume wages evenly distributed)

Problem 2: Multi-State Withholding Analysis

Precision Steel Erectors (based in Indiana) has the following employee situations:

Employee A:

  • Resident of Indiana
  • Works 60% in Indiana, 40% in Michigan
  • Annual wages: $75,000

Employee B:

  • Resident of Pennsylvania
  • Works 100% in Ohio
  • Annual wages: $68,000

Employee C:

  • Resident of Illinois
  • Works 70% in Indiana, 30% in Kentucky
  • Annual wages: $82,000

Required:

  1. Determine which state(s) require income tax withholding for each employee
  2. Identify if reciprocity agreements apply
  3. Calculate withholding amounts (use simplified rates: Indiana 3.15%, Michigan 4.25%, Pennsylvania 3.07%, Ohio 3.5%, Illinois 4.95%, Kentucky 4.5%)
  4. List forms employees must file to claim reciprocity
  5. Describe W-2 reporting requirements (which states on Box 15-17)

Problem 3: Worker Classification Analysis

Evaluate whether the following workers should be classified as employees or independent contractors using the IRS 20-factor test:

Worker 1: Maria - Concrete Finisher

  • Works for ABC Concrete exclusively
  • Arrives at 7 AM daily as directed by foreman
  • Uses ABC's tools and equipment
  • Paid $35/hour every Friday
  • Receives Form 1099-NEC annually
  • ABC sets work sequence and inspects work daily
  • Must personally perform work
  • Can be terminated with 1 week notice
  • Has worked for ABC for 3 years
  • Does not advertise services or have business cards

Worker 2: John - Engineering Consultant

  • Owns JK Engineering LLC
  • Works for 8 different contractors simultaneously
  • Provides structural engineering reviews for specific projects
  • Works from own office using own computer and software
  • Bills monthly for services rendered
  • Carries own professional liability insurance
  • Has 3 employees who assist with projects
  • Licensed professional engineer
  • Contracts specify deliverables but not methods
  • Website advertises services to general public

Required:

  1. Analyze each worker using at least 10 of the 20 IRS factors
  2. Provide classification recommendation (employee vs. independent contractor)
  3. For Worker 1, if misclassified, calculate potential tax exposure (assume $70,000 annual payments over 2 years, FICA 7.65%, FUTA 0.6%, SUTA 2.5%, penalties 25%)
  4. Recommend corrective actions

Problem 4: WOTC Credit Maximization

Rocky Mountain Builders hired the following employees in 2025 and obtained WOTC certifications:

EmployeeTarget GroupHire DateHourly WageHours Worked (First Year)
Robert K.SNAP RecipientJan 15, 2025$22/hour2,080
Susan M.Disabled VeteranFeb 1, 2025$28/hour2,080
David L.Ex-FelonMar 10, 2025$19/hour1,920
Emily R.Summer YouthJun 1, 2025$15/hour480
Michael T.Long-Term WelfareApr 15, 2025$24/hour1,560

Required:

  1. Calculate first-year wages for each employee
  2. Determine applicable credit rate (25% or 40%) based on hours worked
  3. Calculate maximum WOTC credit for each employee
  4. Calculate total WOTC credit for company
  5. Prepare journal entry to record credit when claimed on tax return
  6. Calculate 5-year net benefit if company maintains similar hiring pattern (assume $2,000 annual screening cost)

Key Takeaways - Week 2

Essential Concepts to Remember

  • FICA Taxes: 7.65% employer + 7.65% employee on wages up to SS wage base ($168,600 in 2025); Medicare has no wage cap; Additional Medicare Tax (0.9%) applies to high earners
  • FUTA: Effective rate of 0.6% on first $7,000 per employee after state credit; watch for credit reduction states
  • SUTA: Varies dramatically by state (wage bases from $7,000 to $67,600; rates from 0% to 10%+); experience rating is critical
  • Multi-State Withholding: Withhold for work state unless reciprocity agreement exists; always obtain exemption certificate; report to all states
  • Worker Classification: Use IRS 20-factor test; ABC test in CA/MA/NJ is much stricter; misclassification is extremely costly
  • Section 530: Limited safe harbor if reasonable basis, consistency, and reporting compliance met
  • 1099 Compliance: File by January 31; obtain W-9 before first payment; backup withholding at 24% if no TIN; penalties up to $630 per form
  • WOTC: Worth up to $9,600 per employee; must file Form 8850 within 28 days of hire; systematic screening creates significant value
## Flashcards - Week 2 1. **Q: What is the 2025 Social Security wage base?** **A:** $168,600 - the maximum amount of wages subject to Social Security tax (6.2% employee + 6.2% employer) 2. **Q: What is the effective FUTA rate after maximum state credit?** **A:** 0.6% (6.0% statutory rate minus 5.4% maximum state credit) on first $7,000 of wages per employee annually 3. **Q: Which states have the highest SUI wage bases for 2025?** **A:** Washington ($67,600), Alaska ($47,100), and Wyoming ($30,900) have among the highest wage bases, significantly increasing unemployment tax costs 4. **Q: What is a state reciprocity agreement?** **A:** An agreement between states allowing employees who work in one state but live in another to pay income tax only to their resident state, simplifying withholding 5. **Q: What is the ABC test for worker classification?** **A:** A strict test used in CA, MA, NJ, and other states requiring ALL three conditions: (A) free from control, (B) work outside usual business, (C) independent business established 6. **Q: What is the penalty for late filing of Form 1099-NEC?** **A:** $60 if filed within 30 days late, $120 if 30+ days late, $310 if after August 1 or not filed, $630 for intentional disregard (2025 amounts) 7. **Q: When must backup withholding begin?** **A:** When contractor fails to provide TIN (no Form W-9), IRS issues B-notice of TIN mismatch, or IRS notifies of backup withholding requirement - withhold 24% 8. **Q: What is the maximum Work Opportunity Tax Credit per employee?** **A:** Up to $9,600 for long-term family assistance recipients or disabled veterans; $2,400 for most other target groups; $1,200 for summer youth 9. **Q: What is the deadline to submit Form 8850 for WOTC?** **A:** Within 28 days of employee's start date - missing this deadline disqualifies the employer from claiming the credit even if employee is certified 10. **Q: What is Section 530 Safe Harbor relief?** **A:** Protection from worker reclassification if employer had reasonable basis for contractor treatment, treated workers consistently, and filed all required 1099s timely

questions.question: What is the total FICA tax rate (employee + employer combined) for wages below the Social Security wage base in 2025?
questions.explanation: The combined FICA rate is 15.3%: Social Security is 12.4% (6.2% employee + 6.2% employer) and Medicare is 2.9% (1.45% employee + 1.45% employer). This applies to wages up to the Social Security wage base of $168,600 in 2025.

questions.question: An employee earning $200,000 annually (single filer) will be subject to Additional Medicare Tax withholding of:
questions.explanation: Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to wages over $200,000 for single filers. Since the employee earns exactly $200,000, the threshold is not exceeded, so no Additional Medicare Tax withholding applies. If wages were $205,000, the additional 0.9% would apply to the $5,000 over the threshold.

questions.question: After the maximum state unemployment credit, the effective FUTA rate is:
questions.explanation: The FUTA statutory rate is 6.0%, but employers receive a credit of up to 5.4% for timely state unemployment tax payments, resulting in an effective rate of 0.6% (6.0% - 5.4% = 0.6%). This applies to the first $7,000 of wages per employee, resulting in a maximum FUTA tax of $42 per employee annually.

questions.question: Which state has the highest SUI wage base for 2025?
questions.explanation: Washington has the highest SUI wage base at $67,600 for 2025, which is nearly 10 times higher than California's $7,000 base. This means an employee earning $70,000 would have nearly the entire salary subject to SUI in Washington, versus only the first $7,000 in California, dramatically increasing the employer's unemployment tax burden.

questions.question: A Pennsylvania resident works full-time in Maryland. Which state's income tax should be withheld?
questions.explanation: Pennsylvania and Maryland have a reciprocity agreement. The employee should file Maryland Form MW507 (reciprocity exemption), and the employer should withhold only Pennsylvania tax. Maryland will receive informational wage reporting but no tax withholding. This simplifies compliance and avoids the employee needing to file a Maryland nonresident return.

questions.question: Under the IRS 20-factor test, which factor MOST strongly indicates independent contractor status?
options: Worker is paid by the hour
Worker provides own tools and has significant investment in equipment
Worker must work at company job sites
questions.explanation: Providing own tools and having significant investment in facilities/equipment strongly indicates independent contractor status (factors 14 and 15). Hourly payment indicates employee, working at company sites indicates employee, and receiving training indicates employee. The more significant the worker's investment in their own business, the stronger the case for contractor status.

questions.question: Under California's ABC test, a framing contractor wants to classify carpenters as independent contractors. This classification will:
options: Likely pass all three prongs of the ABC test
Fail prong B because carpentry is the usual course of business
Pass if the carpenters have their own tools
Be allowed if the company files proper 1099s
questions.explanation: The ABC test prong B requires that work be performed outside the usual course of the hiring entity's business. For a framing contractor, carpentry IS the usual course of business, so this classification fails prong B and the workers must be treated as employees. The ABC test is much stricter than the IRS 20-factor test and makes it nearly impossible to classify workers performing core construction services as contractors.

questions.question: What is the deadline to file Form 1099-NEC with the IRS for the 2024 tax year?
questions.explanation: Form 1099-NEC must be filed with the IRS by January 31, 2025 for the 2024 tax year. This is the same deadline for providing copies to recipients. The deadline was accelerated from the previous February/March deadlines to combat fraud and improve tax administration. Missing this deadline results in penalties starting at $60 per form if filed within 30 days.

questions.question: Backup withholding is required at what rate when a contractor fails to provide a valid TIN?
questions.explanation: Backup withholding is required at 24% when a contractor fails to provide a Taxpayer Identification Number, the IRS issues a B-notice of TIN mismatch, or the IRS notifies you the contractor is subject to backup withholding. The withheld amount must be remitted to the IRS using Form 945 and is credited against the contractor's income tax liability.

questions.question: What is the maximum Work Opportunity Tax Credit for hiring a disabled veteran who works 400+ hours and earns $30,000 in the first year?
questions.explanation: The maximum WOTC for hiring a disabled veteran is $9,600 (40% of the first $24,000 in wages, assuming 400+ hours worked). Even though this veteran earned $30,000, only the first $24,000 qualifies for the credit. The 40% rate applies when the employee works 400 or more hours; if they work 120-399 hours, only a 25% rate applies.

questions.question: What is the critical deadline for submitting Form 8850 to claim the Work Opportunity Tax Credit?
questions.explanation: Form 8850 must be submitted to the state workforce agency within 28 days of the employee's start date. Missing this deadline completely disqualifies the employer from claiming the WOTC, even if the employee is a certified member of a target group. This is one of the most common and costly mistakes employers make with WOTC.

questions.question: A construction company with gross receipts of $8 million files 75 Forms 1099-NEC 45 days late. What is the penalty exposure?
questions.explanation: Forms filed more than 30 days late but by August 1 incur a penalty of $120 per form. 75 forms × $120 = $9,000. If filed within 30 days, the penalty would be $60 per form ($4,500 total). If filed after August 1 or not at all, the penalty increases to $310 per form ($23,250 total). Small businesses (≤$5M revenue) have lower maximum penalties, but this company exceeds the threshold.

questions.question: Which of the following can be credited toward Davis-Bacon fringe benefit requirements?
questions.explanation: Only bona fide benefits voluntarily provided to employees can be credited toward Davis-Bacon fringe requirements. Health insurance qualifies. FICA and workers' compensation cannot be credited because they are required by law, not voluntary employer contributions. Other creditable benefits include pension contributions, paid time off, and other voluntary benefit programs.

questions.question: What is Section 530 Safe Harbor relief?
options: Exemption from all payroll taxes for small businesses
Protection from reclassification if specific requirements are met
Reduced penalty for late payroll tax deposits
questions.explanation: Section 530 provides limited relief from worker reclassification if the employer: (1) had a reasonable basis for contractor treatment, (2) treated workers consistently and filed all required 1099s timely, and (3) meets reporting compliance. It does NOT exempt from taxes or approve contractors automatically - it only prevents retroactive reclassification for past periods if requirements are met.

questions.question: New York's 'convenience of employer' rule can result in:
options: Lower tax rates for remote workers
Taxation by New York even if employee works remotely in another state
Exemption from payroll taxes for telecommuters
questions.explanation: New York's convenience rule allows NY to tax income earned by remote workers in other states if the remote arrangement is for the employee's convenience (not employer necessity). This can create double taxation where both NY (work state under convenience rule) and the employee's resident state tax the same income. The employee must claim a credit on one state's return to avoid double taxation.

weeks.title: Week 3: Payroll Tax Strategies & Optimization
weeks.lessonHtml:
Week 3: Workers' Compensation and Employee Benefits

Learning Objectives

By the end of this week, you will be able to:

  • Calculate workers' compensation premiums using class codes and experience modification rates
  • Understand and optimize Experience Modification Rate (EMR) to reduce insurance costs
  • Implement safety programs that directly impact workers' comp expenses
  • Design and account for comprehensive employee benefit packages
  • Allocate benefit costs accurately to construction projects
  • Evaluate retirement plan options for construction companies
  • Navigate ACA compliance and health insurance requirements

Introduction: The Impact of Benefits on Construction Profitability

Employee benefits and workers' compensation insurance represent 15-25% of total payroll costs for construction companies. For a contractor with $10 million in annual payroll, this translates to $1.5-$2.5 million in annual benefit expenses. Strategic management of these costs directly impacts competitiveness and profitability.

Construction Industry Benefit Costs (2025 Averages)

  • Workers' Compensation: 8-15% of payroll (varies by classification)
  • Health Insurance: $650-$950 per employee per month
  • Retirement Contributions: 3-6% of payroll
  • Paid Time Off: 4-6% of payroll
  • Other Benefits: 2-4% of payroll
  • Total Benefit Load: 20-35% of base wages

Section 1: Workers' Compensation Premium Calculations

1.1 Understanding Class Codes

Workers' compensation premiums are calculated based on classification codes that reflect the risk level of different types of work. Each classification has a rate per $100 of payroll.

Common Construction Class Codes and Rates
